query_text: What is biologically happening to your voice when you whisper?

message.content:
When you whisper, several important biological changes occur in your voice production system:

## 1. Vocal Cords Stop Vibrating

The most fundamental difference is that **your vocal cords (vocal folds) do not vibrate during whispering**. In normal speech, air from your lungs passes through the larynx and causes the vocal cords to open and close rapidly, creating periodic vibrations that produce pitch and tone. During whispering, the vocal cords are held in a static, partially open position, which prevents this vibration entirely.

## 2. Glottis Remains Partially Open

In normal speech, your glottis (the opening between the vocal cords) alternates between closed and slightly open as the vocal folds vibrate. When whispering, **the glottis stays permanently partly open**. This requires activation of the posterior cricoarytenoid (PCA) muscle—the main abductor muscle of the larynx—to actively prevent the glottis from closing and to stop vocal fold vibration.

## 3. Turbulent Airflow Creates Sound

Instead of periodic vocal cord vibrations, whispering produces sound through **turbulent airflow**. As air passes through the partially open glottis and between the arytenoid cartilages, it creates audible turbulence. This results in a broadband, noise-like sound rather than the harmonic-rich tone of normal speech. The sound is essentially "white noise" that gets shaped by your vocal tract.

## 4. Loss of Pitch Information

Because there are no vocal cord vibrations, **whispering lacks a fundamental frequency** and the harmonic overtones that give normal speech its pitch characteristics. This is why it's difficult to detect or change pitch when whispering, and why whispered speech has a relatively flat, noise-like spectrum.

## 5. Increased Muscle Tension and Potential Strain

Research has shown that whispering can actually **increase tension in certain laryngeal muscles**. A 2006 fiberoptic study of 100 patients with voice complaints found that 69% demonstrated more severe supraglottic hyperfunction (excessive muscle engagement) when whispering compared to normal speech. Many people squeeze their vocal cords together more tightly to produce a whisper, which can be more traumatic than normal speaking.

## 6. Vocal Tract Reshaping Remains Similar

Despite the different sound source, **your articulatory system (tongue, lips, jaw) still shapes the vocal tract** in essentially the same way as during normal speech. The vocal tract acts as a resonator, enhancing certain frequencies to create formants that distinguish different phonemes. This is why you can still understand whispered words—the spectral shaping by the vocal tract remains, even though the excitation source has changed.

## 7. Drying Effect on Vocal Cords

The continuous airflow during whispering can cause **vocal cords to dry out more quickly** than during regular speech. This drying effect can lead to irritation, which is particularly problematic if you're already experiencing hoarseness or laryngitis.

## Summary

| Aspect | Normal Speech | Whispering |
|--------|-------------|------------|
| Vocal cords | Vibrate periodically | Held partially open, no vibration |
| Sound source | Periodic glottal pulses | Turbulent airflow (noise) |
| Pitch | Present (fundamental frequency) | Absent |
| Glottis | Opens and closes | Stays partially open |
| Muscle activity | Coordinated opening/closing | PCA muscle actively prevents closure |
